title: Shloka 179
subtitle: Ten seals of the hand, and then the seal that is knowledge

namas.translation: The ten mudrās shown with the hands bring her worship to completion.

compound.gloss: to be fully worshipped by means of the ten mudrās

children.gloss: seal, ritual gesture of the hands
to be fully propitiated, worthy of worship

namas.translation: She brings the sovereign splendour of Tripurā under her control, and confers that same mastery on those who worship her.

morphology.note: The first member keeps its accusative -am before karī, an upapada formation of the type vaśaṃkara.

compound.gloss: she who subjugates by the majesty of Tripurā

namas.translation: She is the jñānamudrā, the gesture in which the hand alone says what is understood.

compound.gloss: the seal which is knowledge itself

children.gloss: seal, ritual gesture of the hands

namas.translation: No approach except knowing arrives at her.
She is at once the act of knowledge and the thing it knows, so that in her the two never stand apart.

morphology.note: Since -in carries the having, jñānajñeyasvarūpa is the compound and svarūpiṇī a taddhita on it; the bahuvrīhi reading, she who has knowledge and its object for her form, is equally defensible.

compound.gloss: having knowledge and its object for her own form

children.gloss: that which is to be known
having as her own essential form

commentary.meaning: The verse is built on a single word used twice in two senses. Mudrā is a seal: first the ten seals made with the hands, which complete the worship of the Śrīcakra and by which she is said to be fully propitiated, and then the seal that is not made with the hands at all. Between the two stands a name about power — she brings the splendour of Tripurā under her control — and it is placed there because the fourth of the ten seals is itself called the one that subjugates everything. Then the second line turns, and turns decisively. Three names in a row are built on jñāna: she is the seal of knowledge, she is reached by knowledge, and she is the knowing and the thing known in one form. The hand has been doing the work for a line and a half; now the hymn says that the last gesture is made somewhere else. The names of the ten seals continue into the following verse, so the two verses have to be read as one sequence.
commentary.history:
Mudrā means a seal, in the flatly practical sense: the signet pressed into wax or clay that makes a document official. The word covers the ring, the impression, and by extension any mark of authentication, and only after that does it come to mean the shapes made with the fingers in dance and in worship. Keeping the ordinary sense in view is the best protection against exoticism. When a practitioner shows a mudrā at the end of an offering, what he is doing has the logic of a signature: the rite has been performed, and the hand certifies it. Tantric texts also offer a devotional etymology, deriving the word from mud, joy, and a root meaning to give or to melt, so that a mudrā is what bestows delight or dissolves. That derivation is a piece of theology rather than of philology, but it records accurately enough what the gestures are held to do.

The ten seals are a fixed set in this school. The ritual manuals agree on the number, and largely on the names, and they attach the ten to the enclosures of the Śrīcakra so that each seal belongs to a particular stage of the worship. The list runs through the ones that agitate, disperse, attract, subjugate, madden and goad, and closes with the seal of the sky-goer, the seal of the seed, the seal of the source, and the seal made in three sections. Two things confirm the arrangement from inside the hymn itself. The name that follows immediately here contains vaśaṅkarī, subjugating, which is the fourth of the set; and the next verse opens with yonimudrā and trikhaṇḍeśī, the seal of the source and the mistress of the threefold seal, which are the last two. The stotra is not alluding to the ten seals in passing. It is walking through the end of the list.

Samārādhyā, in the first name, is a gerundive from sam-ā-√rādh, to propitiate completely — she who is to be worshipped, and worshipped to the end. The point of the prefix is completion: the seals are shown when everything else has been done, and without them the tradition regards the worship as unfinished rather than as merely less elaborate.

Tripurāśrīvaśaṅkarī deserves to be read without flinching. Vaśa is control or subjection, and vaśīkaraṇa, bringing under control, is one of the six acts that tantric literature discusses openly and at length — pacifying, subjugating, immobilising, estranging, driving away, and killing. This hymn belongs to a tradition that has such a literature and does not pretend otherwise. What the compound actually says is that she brings the śrī of Tripurā, the sovereign splendour of the goddess of the three cities, under her own control, and the tradition's ordinary extension of such names is that what she controls she can confer. The same texts that describe the six acts insist that the practitioner who wants any of them has settled for very little, and the placement of this name is a small instance of that argument: it is the last thing said about power before the hymn changes the subject entirely.

The change is the second line. Jñānamudrā names a gesture that anyone would recognise on an image of the teaching Śiva or a seated sage — thumb and forefinger brought into a circle, the other three fingers open — but the compound is a karmadhāraya, the seal that is knowledge itself, which takes the name past the description of a hand. Jñānagamyā then says she is reached by knowledge, and the word gamyā is an ordinary gerundive of √gam, to go: she is arrived at that way and not another. And then the third name withdraws the instrument it has just offered. If she is jñānajñeyasvarūpiṇī, having knowledge and the object of knowledge for her own form, then knowledge is not a road that leads to her, because both ends of the road are already she. The sequence is not careless. It gives the practitioner a method and then removes the distance the method was meant to cross, which is the standard shape of this argument wherever it appears in Indian philosophy, and the reason the verse ends where it does.
commentary.practice:
Everything in this verse depends on one cluster. Jñā occurs four times in the second line, and jñ is the sound that divides reciters more than any other in Sanskrit. Written, it is unambiguous: the voiced palatal stop j followed by the palatal nasal ñ. Spoken, it is regional. Much of northern India says something close to gya, Maharashtra says dnya, and the south commonly says gnya. None of these communities is reciting badly; they are transmitting the pronunciation they received. But a learner should know what the two letters are before choosing which tradition to follow, and should at least once try the strict value, j and ñ made at the same palatal position with no gap, to feel why the spelling is what it is.

With that settled, the second line becomes the best drill in the hymn for the palatal series. Jñānamudrā jñānagamyā jñānajñeyasvarūpiṇī gives you jñā, jñā, jñā, jñe in quick succession, and the fourth changes only its vowel. Take the line at half speed, keep the ā long in every jñāna, and let the e of jñeya be a full long vowel rather than the short English e.

The first line has two other clusters. In vaśaṅkarī the ṅ is the guttural nasal, made where the k is made, and the word is properly vaśaṃ-karī with the accusative preserved inside the compound — a formation the grammarians treat as a class of its own, and one worth recognising because the hymn uses it more than once. In tripurāśrī the śrī is palatal ś, then r, then long ī, all three sounded; it is not shree with the vowel of English see.

Samārādhyā is built from sam plus ā plus the root, and the ending dhy is an aspirated dental followed by the palatal glide, d with breath running into y and no vowel between them. Svarūpiṇī closes the verse with a retroflex ṇ, which is retroflex because of the r earlier in the word, the same rule that governs tarpaṇa in the previous verse.

For archanā the five datives are daśamudrāsamārādhyāyai, tripurāśrīvaśaṅkaryai, jñānamudrāyai, jñānagamyāyai, jñānajñeyasvarūpiṇyai. Note that the two ī-stems, vaśaṅkarī and svarūpiṇī, contract to -ryai and -ṇyai, while the ā-stems keep the full -āyai.

What the verse asks depends on how you are using it. If you perform the Śrīcakra worship, the ten seals are shown at fixed points and this verse is a mnemonic for the end of that list; the two verses together will take you through it. If you are only reciting, the second line is still addressed to you, and it asks something more demanding than a gesture. It says that the last seal is not something you do with your hands, and that whatever knowing you bring to the recitation is not a tool you are using on her.

crossReferences.source: Bhagavad Gītā, chapter 13 (numbered 13.17 in editions that do not count Arjuna's opening question, 13.18 in those that do)
crossReferences.deva: ज्योतिषामपि तज्ज्योतिस्तमसः परमुच्यते । ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं ज्ञानगम्यं हृदि सर्वस्य विष्ठितम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: jyotiṣām api taj jyotis tamasaḥ param ucyate | jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ jñānagamyaṃ hṛdi sarvasya viṣṭhitam ||
crossReferences.translation: That is the light even of lights; it is said to be beyond darkness. It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and what is to be reached by knowledge, seated in the heart of every being.
crossReferences.relevance: The three names of the second line are this verse rearranged into the feminine. The Gītā puts jñānam, jñeyam and jñānagamyam in a single line; the sahasranāma gives jñānagamyā and jñānajñeyasvarūpiṇī as two consecutive names of the goddess. Whether the hymn is quoting or drawing on a shared formula cannot be settled, but a reader should know that this line is old and famous, and that the stotra's phrasing would have been heard as an echo.

crossReferences.deva: यद्वाचानभ्युदितं येन वागभ्युद्यते । तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥
crossReferences.iast: yad vācānabhyuditaṃ yena vāg abhyudyate | tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate ||
crossReferences.translation: What is not uttered by speech, and by which speech is uttered — know that alone to be brahman, and not this that people here worship.
crossReferences.relevance: The classical warning that goes with jñānagamyā. The Upaniṣad grants that there is a knowing which reaches the absolute and in the same breath denies that the absolute can be set in front of the knower as an object, which is precisely the correction the hymn applies one name later with jñānajñeyasvarūpiṇī. The last clause is also uncomfortable and should be left uncomfortable: it says that what is worshipped as an object is not it.

references.title: Hindu Tantrism
references.author: Sanjukta Gupta, Dirk Jan Hoens and Teun Goudriaan (Handbuch der Orientalistik, Brill, 1979)
references.note: Gupta's long chapter on tantric ritual is the most sober description in English of what mudrās are for and where they fall in the order of worship. Dry, technical, and exactly what is needed to stop the ten seals from sounding like a mystery when they are in fact a procedure.

references.title: Māyā Divine and Human
references.author: Teun Goudriaan (Motilal Banarsidass, 1978)
references.note: A study of the Indian vocabulary of power and illusion that includes a careful treatment of the six acts, vaśīkaraṇa among them. Read it before deciding what to make of vaśaṅkarī: the material is neither hidden by the tradition nor central to it, and Goudriaan is unusually good at holding both facts at once.

references.title: Eight Upaniṣads, with the Commentary of Śaṅkarācārya
references.author: tr. Swami Gambhirananda (Advaita Ashrama, 2 vols)
references.note: The most usable bilingual edition of the Kena and its companions. Śaṅkara's comment on the first section is the classical discussion of how something can be reached by knowledge without becoming an object of it, which is the exact difficulty the second line of this verse creates and then resolves.

references.title: The Bhagavad Gītā, translated and interpreted
references.author: Franklin Edgerton (Harvard Oriental Series 38–39, 1944)
references.note: Edgerton prints the Sanskrit facing a deliberately unliterary English, which is what you want when checking a half-line like jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ jñānagamyam against the hymn. His second volume is also a clear-headed account of how the Gītā's vocabulary was later put to uses the poem did not anticipate.
